title: How accurate is this?
intro: Measured on datasets, not on astronauts. Every number comes from a test or report in tools/ that anyone can re-run.

results.result: 0.16 per crew-day, about one every 6 days per crew (91 alerts in 567 crew-days; crew A 0.05, B 0.15, C 0.25, D 0.20). Was 0.11 before the shared replays added steps and soreness and crew D became PMData p10, who also answers the daily wellness questions; most extra alerts are on those self-reported scores
results.measured_on: 4 shared crew replays in replay/ built from PMData (Earth wearable data, 16 people, CC BY 4.0)

results.result: starting values in tools/test_detection.py (0.20 on the first replays)
results.rerun: The same command as the row above

results.result: A +10 bpm rise over 9 days is caught on day 8. The planned +6 bpm over 9 days is not reliably caught: it is smaller than normal life swings in this data.
results.measured_on: Calm crew (PMData p01) with the drift added

results.result: Fires at the first VT/VF/PEA/asystole reading, or heart rate ≥150 or <50 bpm for 30 s with systolic BP <90 mmHg
results.measured_on: Stream in the Pulse emergency replay's format

results.result: 4.9 bpm mean error; 67 % of 20 s windows within 5 bpm
results.measured_on: 5 consenting UBFC-rPPG people, 12 windows (research use only)

results.result: Mean error 1.12 points on a 0–10 scale, the same as "tomorrow = today" (1.12); range covers the true answer 89.6 % of the time (target about 90 %)
results.measured_on: 16 PMData people, each forecast only for people never used to train

labels: every detection cut-off is a "team value" or an "Earth reference, no space data" (sources in `content/profiles/detection-cut-offs.json`). The forecast and webcam numbers are "estimate, not validated".
limits: Accuracy is measured on datasets, not on astronauts. Real-time performance with real astronauts may differ.
No open astronaut wearable stream exists. Normal days come from Earth wearable data (PMData) shaped to look like a crew.
Detection has no training step, so no person was "seen in training". But the cut-offs were tuned on the same four crews they are measured on, so the false-alert number is optimistic.
On real Earth data, people's resting heart rate moves by several bpm over weeks without any illness. A slow drift has to be larger than that to be caught reliably.
The emergency is a Pulse Physiology Engine simulation ("estimate, not validated"). Chest pain is crew-reported, not simulated.

Safety limits are Earth clinical references (AHA). There are no published in-flight limits. A low heart rate can be normal for fit people, so the low limit is applied to the live heart rate only, not to resting heart rate.
Webcam heart rate was measured on 5 people in good light, sitting still. One person had errors of 8–20 bpm.
The readiness forecast is no more accurate than assuming tomorrow equals today. Its value is the range and the explanation, not the number.
